Roofing Academic and Research Buildings at Wake Forest, WSSU, and Salem College

Winston-Salem carries three very different campuses inside a few miles of each other. Wake Forest University's research and athletic facilities, Winston-Salem State University's public-institution building stock, and Salem College's historic downtown core each come with their own roofing constraints, and a contractor who treats them the same way will misjudge the schedule, the materials, or the approval process on at least one of them.

Historic Buildings vs. Modern Research Space

Salem College's older academic buildings sit inside a designated historic district, which means roof replacement is both a membrane decision and a visual-compatibility decision reviewed against the district's standards for roofline, material, and color. Slate and standing-seam metal on those buildings gets repaired and matched rather than replaced wholesale wherever the existing material can be salvaged, and any full replacement goes through a submittal process that documents the historic profile being preserved.

A few miles away, lab and research buildings tied to Wake Forest's programs and the Innovation Quarter's academic-affiliated space are almost entirely low-slope membrane roofs carrying heavy rooftop mechanical loads — fume hood exhaust, lab air handlers, backup power infrastructure. Those roofs get engineered for equipment weight and vibration first, historic compatibility never enters the conversation.

Working Around the Academic Calendar

Dormitory and classroom roof work gets scheduled around the academic calendar as a matter of course. Summer break, between spring commencement and fall move-in, is when we do the bulk of steep-slope dormitory reroofing and any tear-off work that would otherwise disrupt classes in session. Research buildings that run experiments year-round don't get that luxury, so lab roof work gets phased and coordinated with the building's research schedule regardless of the calendar month.

Athletic facility roofs follow yet another calendar — field house and arena roofs get scheduled around the competition and event calendar, since a home game or a commencement ceremony under a leaking roof is not a risk any athletic department or facilities director wants to explain afterward.

  • Historic district submittal for any Salem College roof visible from the street
  • Structural review before adding rooftop lab exhaust or research equipment
  • Summer-window scheduling for occupied dormitory and classroom buildings
  • Event-calendar coordination for athletic and assembly facility roofs
  • Public bid documentation for WSSU capital projects
  • Moisture survey before any recover on aging academic building stock

Lab Exhaust, Fume Hoods, and Rooftop Penetrations

Research buildings accumulate rooftop penetrations over decades of grant-funded lab build-outs, and by the time a roof reaches replacement age it often carries far more curbs, stacks, and exhaust points than the original roof plan shows. We map every existing penetration before design, flash each one to the manufacturer's detail for chemical and fume exhaust where applicable, and coordinate any temporary shutdown of lab exhaust with the research staff running active experiments underneath.

Fume hood exhaust stacks in particular need corrosion-resistant flashing details, since the exhaust stream can degrade standard metal flashing faster than ordinary weather exposure would. We spec flashing material against the specific exhaust chemistry where the university's environmental health and safety office can tell us what's running through a given stack.

Dormitory and Athletic Facility Roofs

Dormitory roofs — whether steep-slope shingle or low-slope membrane depending on the building era — get evaluated for life-cycle cost against a compressed maintenance window, since housing operations can't absorb an open roof deck once students move back in. Athletic facility roofs, particularly larger clear-span structures, carry their own wind uplift and drainage engineering given the roof area and the open interior volume underneath.

Capital Planning and Procurement for Campus Facilities

WSSU, as a public university, runs roofing projects through state procurement and public bid requirements, and we build submittals to match that process — itemized scope, prevailing documentation, and a bid package that gives the university's facilities office everything it needs for board or state approval. Wake Forest and Salem College, as private institutions, typically run a more direct RFP process through their own facilities departments, but still expect the same rigor in product data sheets, warranty terms, and as-built documentation at closeout.

Across all three, capital planning teams want a roof condition assessment that feeds a multi-year budget cycle rather than a quote for a single upcoming project. We provide that assessment as part of any campus-wide roofing engagement so facilities directors can sequence buildings by actual remaining service life rather than by which roof is leaking loudest this year.

Common Questions From Campus Facilities Offices

Does a historic district review add significant time to a Salem College roof project?

It adds a submittal step, but we build that into the schedule from the start so it doesn't become a surprise delay once the project is already underway.

Can lab building roof work happen without shutting down research?

In most cases, yes. We coordinate any exhaust or utility interruption directly with the research staff and schedule around active experiment cycles wherever possible.

How does WSSU's public procurement process differ from a private university's?

WSSU projects run through state bid requirements with formal documentation at each stage. Wake Forest and Salem College typically manage the process directly through their facilities departments with more flexibility on scheduling and vendor selection.

What roof systems hold up best on dormitory buildings?

It depends on the building era and slope. Steep-slope dormitories generally do well with architectural shingle or standing-seam metal, while flat-roof residence halls are usually TPO or modified bitumen sized for the expected foot traffic from move-in and move-out.

Do you provide a multi-year roof condition assessment for capital planning?

Yes. We survey each building's roof condition and remaining service life so a facilities office can sequence replacement across a campus rather than reacting building by building.
